title: Objects and Instances
summary: Turn blueprints into reality! Learn how to create real objects using the 'new' keyword, set their data, and call their methods.
learningObjectives: Learn the exact Java syntax to create an object: ClassName obj = new ClassName();
Understand what the 'new' keyword does in simple language
Access an object's fields and methods using the dot (.) operator
Realize that an 'instance' is simply another word for an actual object
expectedOutcomes: Confidence creating objects and setting their properties independently
Ability to answer the classic question: 'If Student is a class, is student1 the class?'

activities.title: The Cookie Cutter vs The Baked Cookie

analogy.headline: One cookie cutter can make a dozen real cookies
analogy.story:
Think of a star-shaped cookie cutter in a bakery.

The metal cookie cutter is the **Class (Blueprint)**. It defines the shape, the size, and the sharp edges.

When you press it into dough and bake it, you get a real, edible cookie you can hold and eat! That delicious cookie is an **Object (Instance)**.

If you make a second cookie, it comes from the same cutter, but it is a completely separate cookie. You could put chocolate sprinkles on cookie #1 and powdered sugar on cookie #2. Neither cookie interferes with the other.

That is exactly how objects work in Java!
analogy.keyTakeaway: You define the class once. Then you can use the 'new' keyword to create as many real objects from it as you want.

activities.title: Creating an Object with 'new'
activities.content:
To create a real object from your class blueprint, Java gives you the **`new`** keyword:

```java
Student student1 = new Student();
```

Let's break down this one line word by word — it is much simpler than it looks!

1. **`Student`** (The Type): Just like `int` or `String`, this tells Java what kind of thing `student1` will refer to.
2. **`student1`** (The Variable Name): The name we choose so we can talk to our object.
3. **`=`** (Assignment): Links our variable name to the newly created object.
4. **`new`** (The Creator): The command that tells Java: *"Allocate and create a brand new object right now!"*
5. **`Student()`**: Tells Java which blueprint to use to set up the object.

---

### Setting Data Using the Dot (`.`) Operator
Once the object is created, how do we give it a name or call its methods? Using the **dot operator (`.`)**:

```java
// Setting properties:
student1.name = "Rahul";
student1.age = 20;
student1.course = "Java";

// Calling behavior:
student1.displayProfile();
```

### Crucial Question:
> *If `Student` is a class, is `student1` the class?*

**Answer: Absolutely NOT!**
- `Student` is the class (the blueprint).
- `student1` is a variable holding a reference to a real `Student` object (an instance).

activities.title: Creating and Using Two Distinct Objects
activities.description:
Look at the terminal output when this runs:
'Student: Rahul | Age: 20 | Course: Java'
'Student: Priya | Age: 21 | Course: Python'
Both objects were created from the single Student class, but each holds its own unique data!

questions.prompt: What keyword is used in Java to create a new object from a class?
questions.explanation: The 'new' keyword instructs the Java runtime to create a new instance of the specified class.

questions.prompt: What operator is used to access an object's fields or call its methods?
questions.explanation: In Java, you access fields and methods of an object using the dot operator (for example: student1.name or student1.displayProfile()).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a class and an object?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A class is a blueprint or template that defines properties and behaviors. An object is a concrete instance created from that blueprint that holds actual data in memory. For example, 'Car' is a class, while your specific red Honda Civic parked outside is an object.
keyPoints: Class = Blueprint / Definition (created once in code)
Object = Instance / Real Entity (created at runtime with 'new')
Multiple objects can be created from a single class
commonMistakes: Using overly technical terms without providing a clear real-world example like Dog vs myPetDog.

activities.title: Lesson 4 Checkpoint
checklist: I know how to write 'ClassName obj = new ClassName();' without looking at notes.
I can set variables and call methods using the dot (.) operator.
I can explain why 'instance' and 'object' mean the same thing.

practiceProblems.title: Create a Mobile Phone Object
practiceProblems.description: Given a Mobile class with String brand and double price, create an object in Main, set brand to 'Pixel 8' and price to 699.99, then print 'Purchased Pixel 8 for $699.99'.
practiceProblems.hint: Use Mobile m = new Mobile(); and then set m.brand and m.price.
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Instantiate a Mobile object, set its brand and price, and print the purchase message.
hints: Remember to use the 'new' keyword to create the object.

practiceProblems.title: Invoke an Object Method
practiceProblems.description: Create a Dog class with String name and a method void bark() that prints: '[name] says Woof!'. In Main, create a Dog with name 'Buddy' and call bark().
practiceProblems.hint: Inside bark(), use: System.out.println(name + " says Woof!");
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Create a Dog object, assign its name, and call its bark() method.
